newsitem.title: USA: Clinton tobacco task force hears nicotine concern.
newsitem.headline: Clinton tobacco task force hears nicotine concern.

text.p: President Clinton's task force reviewing the tobacco settlement on Wednesday heard scientists raise concerns that a key aim of the pact, to eliminate nicotine in cigarettes, may pose unintended risks.

The special task force -- headed by Donna Shalala, Health and Human Services secretary, and White House domestic policy aide Bruce Reed -- met at the White House with scientists concerned about the long-range impact of the complex agreement.

"We talked a great deal about some of the tougher interests," Reed said. "We learned that reducing nicotine may or may not advance the public health. We learned that producing so-called less-hazardous cigarettes may or may not be a desirable result."

Shalala said after the meeting with scientists that, "What they are telling us is that perhaps we need to look at a more sophisticated strategy than perhaps what is in the existing document that we're reviewing.

"We haven't come to any conclusions yet," the cabinet officer stressed in assessing the accord, under which the industry would curb sales practices and pay out $368 billion over 25 years, some of it for financing public health and anti-smoking programs.
One major concession by the industry in the landmark accord is recognition that the Food and Drug Administration has regulatory power over tobacco products.

Under the agreement, the FDA would have the authority to approve all ingredients in tobacco products and standards for reducing harmful components, including nicotine. After 12 years, the FDA could eliminate nicotine entirely from cigarettes.
The proposed agreement mandates testing of ingredients and safety assessments.
"People smoke in order to get nicotine and they get all of these toxins that ultimately kill them as a side effect," said Saul Shiffman of the University of Pittsburgh.

"So one of the dangers is that if you reduce the delivery of nicotine from cigarettes, people have to smoke more of them, smoke them more deeply and therefore may actually increase their burden of mortality and morbidity," he said.
"It is an issue that needs to be handled very carefully," Shiffman said.

Other scientists who participated in the meeting included John Henningfield of Johns Hopkins University, Kenneth Warner of the University of Michigan, Lynn Kozlowski of Penn State and William Rickert, who headed a tobacco study by the Canadian government.
